article.headline: HeyGen's Avatar IV Brings Gesture-Controlled Lip Sync to AI Video
article.lede: HeyGen, a synthetic-video startup that lets users generate talking-head footage without cameras or actors, has updated its Avatar IV model with full-angle lip sync and prompt-driven gesture control. The release marks a meaningful step beyond the first Avatar IV version, which was already praised for accurate mouth movement. The new features let a single still photograph animate into a speaking figure with coordinated body motion.
article.body:
The Avatar IV update addresses one of the persistent embarrassments of AI video: lip sync that looks plausible from the front but falls apart in three-quarter or profile views. HeyGen says the new model maintains **accurate lip movement from all angles**, a claim corroborated by several developers in the research sources who describe the result as approaching uncanny-valley territory — a backhanded compliment that nonetheless signals how far the technology has moved.

The more novel addition is *gesture control*, which allows users to prompt the avatar to perform physical movements — a nod, a raised hand, an expressive shrug — in sync with the spoken script. Combined with the single-photo-to-video capability, a marketer or educator can now take a headshot and produce a fully animated presenter without a production set. HeyGen's platform reports having generated more than 128 million videos to date, suggesting a substantial existing user base that will have immediate access to the upgrade.

HeyGen operates in a crowded field that includes Synthesia, D-ID, and Runway, all of which offer overlapping avatar or video-generation features. What distinguishes this release is the bundling of multi-angle lip sync, gesture prompting, and single-image animation in one update — capabilities that had previously required separate tools or significant manual compositing. The company supports over 300 AI voices across 175 languages, which positions the product heavily toward localization and global marketing workflows.

The practical risks are worth naming. Convincing multi-angle lip sync from a single photo lowers the production barrier for synthetic impersonation. HeyGen has consent requirements for avatar creation using real likenesses, but enforcement at scale remains an open question across the industry. The technology's legitimate uses — training videos, multilingual content, accessibility tools — are genuine, but each capability improvement also sharpens the potential for misuse.

concepts.definition: A technique in which machine-learning models alter or generate mouth movements in video so they match a given audio track. Early systems were limited to frontal views; newer models attempt to maintain coherence as the face turns in three dimensions.

The ability to instruct a synthetic avatar to perform body or hand movements via text prompts, rather than requiring motion-capture data or manual keyframing. The avatar's gestures are generated by the model to match the pacing and intent of the spoken script.

A concept from robotics and animation describing the discomfort humans feel when a synthetic figure looks almost — but not quite — human. In AI video, the term is often used, as here, to indicate that synthetic output has become realistic enough to unsettle viewers.

A generative AI workflow that takes one static image of a person and produces a video clip in which that figure appears to speak and move. The model infers three-dimensional structure, lighting, and motion from the single frame.
